newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - Singapore dollar weakness seen persisting.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Singapore dollar weakness seen persisting.

text.p: The newly beleaguered Singapore dollar could be in for a spell of sustained weakness if the U.S. dollar stays bullish internationally and turmoil in Asian currency markets persists, economists said on Wednesday.

The Singapore dollar fell to an early low of 1.5175 to the U.S. dollar, levels not seen since July 1994, before talk of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) near that level prompted a slight recovery.
It stood at 1.5140/50 at 0910 GMT, but foreign exchange dealers and analysts said it could slide towards the 1.53, and eventually, 1.55 levels.

The latest bout of selling of the usually sturdy Singapore dollar was attributed to an MAS official's comments that the current Singapore dollar level was appropriate to what was happening in the market.

The official of the de facto central bank told reporters on Tuesday that the U.S. dollar had been rising in currency markets and the Singapore dollar had depreciated by about five percent against the U.S. unit since the start of 1997.
Her comments sparked active sales of the Singapore dollar, pushing it abruptly through the psychological support level of 1.50 against the U.S. dollar.
"Obviously, those comments gave the market a green light," said Daniel Lian, head of Asian bond and currency research at NatWest Markets.
But he said market players, particularly large hedge funds, had already been gearing up to test the 1.50 level.
"What the funds in New York are tracking very closely is our export numbers and whether we can convincingly tell them we're able to engineer a recovery in exports," Lian said.
Singapore's non-oil exports, long used to double-digit growth, have been struggling with a downturn in global electronics demand since last year.
Non-oil domestic exports expanded by 4.4 percent in the second quarter of 1997 after contracting 4.1 percent in the previous quarter, according to the latest official figures.
Electronics account for around 70 percent of Singapore's non-oil exports.
Most economists said the Singapore dollar's weakness could help exports while having only a mild inflationary impact.

"Given the benign state of international price trends now, there's further potental for the Singapore dollar to weaken in the medium term without threatening a large rise in price instability," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currency research at BZW Asia.

He said Singapore's policy of managing its exchange rate on a trade-weighted basis made a weakening of its currency inevitable in the context of a robust U.S. dollar and declines in neigbouring currencies after the effective devaluations of the Thai baht and Philippine peso last month.

"We could quite easily see the weakness extending to the 1.55 levels further down the line. And I wouldn't view that as a sign the MAS was diluting its commitment to keeping inflation low," Supple said.
But Jacqueline Ong, economist at independent research house I.D.E.A., said a decline to the 1.55 level would be overdone in view of Singapore's sound fundamentals.
"On a trade-weighted basis, levels from 1.48 to 1.51 may be a little bit painful in terms of making imports more expensive," Ong said.
"If we're talking about prolonged weakness, I think 1.50 is already the limit," she added.
